title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We explicitly state that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. We present the artifact‑backed execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, and give concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to expose generator×guard interactions in future runs.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly explored for intent→configuration tasks in NetOps, where operator intent is translated into device configurations and staged-change procedures (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollback). Prior literature reports that LLMs can synthesize plausible configurations but also emphasizes gaps in operational evaluation: safety depends on end‑to‑end behavior that includes generation, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, rollback, and provenance. We preregistered a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) to probe whether a deterministic runtime validator meaningfully changes end‑to‑end safety outcomes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline under a compact, action‑aware staging benchmark.

Research question. Under the preregistered ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline); the entire experimental design and analysis plan were frozen before execution.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, with archived execution and analysis artifacts that transparently support all principal numbers; (2) an explicit, artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and guard/scorer conflation caused a deterministic ceiling effect in this run, making the primary estimand uninformative; (3) concrete benchmark‑hardening recommendations derived from archived traces; (4) compact, artifact‑grounded execution and statistical summaries to enable reproducible follow‑on experiments.
sections.related_work: Prior work demonstrates intent translation pipelines and LLM‑based generation for network configuration in prototype and benchmark settings (intent‑based configuration, PreConfig, GraphSynth). In infrastructure‑as‑code (IaC) domains, verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops (e.g., TerraFormer) improve correctness for provisioning tasks. Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools have been used to detect configuration and policy errors offline and in emulated environments. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM workflows (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are increasingly applied to AIOps/NetOps but create new failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Surveys highlight a gap: community‑accepted, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our evaluation operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility within these constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We preregistered the study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). The design fixed a paired binary outcome across exactly N=400 tasks with the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline estimand. The confirmatory procedure was a permutation‑based paired difference test (two‑sided, α=0.05) implemented by the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor; an exact McNemar two‑sided test corroborates the primary inference. Bootstrap percentile CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary summaries.

Adapter semantics, shared generation, and model‑call accounting. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Crucially, preregistered semantics set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): the adapter requested one deterministic LLM generation per task and delivered that identical candidate to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This choice isolates validator acceptance behavior on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions. The preregistration documented this semantic and its interpretive scope. As a consequence of shared_initial_generation, the run used model_calls_used = 400 (one shared LLM generation per task) while completing 800 episodes (two episodes per task).

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter: (a) requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini; (b) delivered it to the baseline and guarded episodes; (c) in the guarded episode, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full intent‑constraint validation and either accepted, blocked, or (where configured) invoked a single repair attempt per the preregistered repair policy. The same deterministic implementation served both as the runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer. Validator traces record repair_applied flags, normalized configurations, validation_before/after states, and difficulty metadata for every episode.

Deterministic replay, exclusions, and missingness handling. The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks: each agent+simulator pair was replayed three times; tasks with non‑identical replay outcomes or simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from primary analysis. The registered missingness plan specified automated deterministic exclusion without human adjudication; flagged counts and reasons must be reported. In this run all deterministic consistency checks passed; no exclusions were applied.

Statistical analysis and reproducibility. Primary inference used the preregistered permutation test on paired binary outcomes with exact p‑value reporting and Cohen's h effect size. Secondary summaries included bootstrap percentile CIs for paired differences (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) and descriptive failure‑mode clustering where applicable. All analysis code, seeds, and artifacts are archived in the execution and analysis bundles; deterministic reconciliation and provider‑call audits are included in the archived manifest.

sections.discussion:
Construct‑validity diagnosis and why the primary estimand was uninformative. The deterministic ceiling outcome arises from two preregistered design choices: (1) shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded episodes, and (2) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the validator deterministically accepted the shared candidate for every task, both conditions necessarily produced identical acceptances and post‑hoc scores, yielding n_11 = 400 and zero discordant pairs. In short, the run measured validator acceptance on identical candidate strings rather than independent generator+guard closed‑loop dynamics; under these semantics the preregistered primary estimand cannot detect generator×guard interactions.

Implications for preregistration, power, and interpretation. The original power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability; the observed deterministic ceiling invalidates those assumptions and collapses uncertainty estimates. The permutation and McNemar tests correctly reflect identical outcomes (p = 1.0). Researchers should therefore not interpret the null result as evidence that runtime verification is universally unnecessary—the result is a direct artifact of frozen design choices and implementation homogeneity.

Concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden action‑aware benchmarks. Based on archived traces and the preregistration, we recommend the following implementable steps for future confirmatory runs: (A) set independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output and runtime guards can alter outcomes; (B) avoid conflating runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—use heterogeneous implementations or independent scorers to enable independent adjudication; (C) inject a controlled fraction of perturbation/adversarial seeds (specified in preregistration) to guarantee a measurable baseline failure rate for power calculations; (D) enable and record repair invocations and repair outcomes in adapter traces to produce measurable divergence in rollback/repair statistics; (E) adopt difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversample very_hard patterns so the benchmark contains sufficient error rates to support confirmatory detection.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: this run used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across different LLMs, verifier implementations, or production heterogeneity. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture all production telemetry noise or adversarial actor behaviors. Construct validity: reusing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer conflates acceptance and scoring. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Reproducibility and how to replay the confirmatory analysis. All runtime calls, raw LLM responses, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, per‑task manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts: execution/execution_manifest.json (execution summary and model_calls_used), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (paired outcomes), analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg (bootstrap distribution), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (analysis parameters), and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (per‑task difficulty labels). Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pairs = 400 and that all deterministic consistency checks passed. The archived analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 with the frozen seeds reproduces the reported permutation p, bootstrapped CI, and contingency counts exactly.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator such that both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect is an artifact of preregistered design choices that removed opportunities for the runtime guard to alter outcomes; it does not imply that runtime verification lacks utility in heterogeneous, independently generated, adversarial, or production settings. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce the run and use these artifacts to design hardened experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors in future confirmatory studies.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for the full sample is derivable from that manifest but was not embedded inline in the original text. Representative sample difficulty counts (first six tasks) are included in the Results section to illustrate benchmark diversity.
